title: In NEOWISE 2014-2024, one third of centroid-clean field dwarfs with extreme dust and a 4.6 um excess have variable 1000 K dust, as often as young extreme debris discs; the mean excess does not fade
abstract: Question: Does the hot dust of genuine extreme-dust field dwarfs, the class that contains the known dust dimmers, vary at 3-5 um like young extreme debris discs (EDDs), and does it fade? Approach: We reduced NEOWISE-R (2014-2024) and AllWISE (2010-2011) W1/W2 visits for 951 Gaia DR3 dwarfs with a confirmed 12 um excess (with published centroid-offset blend classes), 1,540 unconfirmed excess stars and 2,889 W1-matched controls. A star is variable when its W2 variability statistics exceed the 99th percentile of magnitude-matched controls. Injections of disc-flux variability into control light curves calibrate the sensitivity. Results: 20 of 180 centred (unblended-like) excess stars are variable (2.1 expected), against 2.2-3.3 percent of blends. For centred stars with a W2 excess of at least 20 percent of the photosphere, 16 of 49 are variable (0.6 expected); 6 of 33 with field kinematics are variable, and 4 of these 33 (G4466 included) change smoothly over years, against 1 of 2,889 controls. The variable flux has a colour temperature near 1000 K (blends: 730-770 K). Half of the variable centred stars have Gaia G scatter above 3 times that of controls, against 7.5 percent of constant ones (p = 8e-6). The fraction of discs with W2 disc rms of at least 20 percent is 0.48 (95 percent upper limit 0.63), and 0.31 (0.50) for field kinematics. Young EDDs give 7 of 17, so the two populations agree. The mean excess trend is -0.01 +- 0.09 percent per year, so the hot dust does not fade on average over 2010-2024. We list three new mature stars with smooth hot-dust changes like G4466. Limitations: statistical blend classes, velocity-only ages, photospheric colours without spectra, W1/W2 only.
